---
title: "Comparing two independent means"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

When groups contain different sampled speakers, there is no within-speaker covariance to exploit. We compare /I/ duration in *hid* between the adult men and adult women in the Hillenbrand cohort. The estimand is the difference in group means,

$$
\Delta=\mu_{\mathrm{man}}-\mu_{\mathrm{woman}},
$$

estimated by

$$
\widehat\Delta=\overline Y_{\mathrm{man}}-\overline Y_{\mathrm{woman}}.
$$

We first derive Welch's standard error for unequal group variances, then calculate the interval from the observed speaker measurements, and finally return to the independence and population assumptions that license that interpretation.

The derivation reuses the [variance--covariance identity](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd), the fact that [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) makes the between-group covariance zero, and the definition of a [standard error](standard-errors.qmd) as the standard deviation of an estimator's sampling distribution.

## Welch's standard error

In general,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\overline Y_m-\overline Y_w]
=
\operatorname{Var}[\overline Y_m]
+\operatorname{Var}[\overline Y_w]
-2\operatorname{Cov}(\overline Y_m,\overline Y_w).
$$

For independent groups, the covariance term is zero, so

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat\Delta]
=\operatorname{Var}[\overline Y_{\mathrm{man}}]
+\operatorname{Var}[\overline Y_{\mathrm{woman}}],
$$

so the estimated standard error is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\Delta)
=\sqrt{\frac{s_m^2}{n_m}+\frac{s_w^2}{n_w}}.
$$

Welch's approximation uses

$$
\nu=
\frac{(s_m^2/n_m+s_w^2/n_w)^2}
{(s_m^2/n_m)^2/(n_m-1)+(s_w^2/n_w)^2/(n_w-1)}
$$

degrees of freedom. It does not require equal group variances.

Welch's procedure is the default here because it allows the two speaker groups to have different variances and sample sizes. The Satterthwaite value $\nu$ chooses a Student-t reference whose uncertainty approximates the uncertainty in the two separately estimated variance contributions. A pooled procedure may be slightly more efficient if equal population variances are genuinely justified, but that extra assumption is not supplied by the study design.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-welch
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
hid <- subset(vowels, vowel == "I" & speaker_type %in% c("man", "woman"),
              select = c(speaker_id, speaker_type, duration_ms))
men <- subset(hid, speaker_type == "man")$duration_ms
women <- subset(hid, speaker_type == "woman")$duration_ms

v_m <- var(men) / length(men)
v_w <- var(women) / length(women)
estimate <- mean(men) - mean(women)
se <- sqrt(v_m + v_w)
df <- (v_m + v_w)^2 /
  (v_m^2 / (length(men) - 1L) + v_w^2 / (length(women) - 1L))
t_observed <- estimate / se
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_observed), df) # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
interval <- estimate + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, df) * se

check <- t.test(men, women, var.equal = FALSE)
stopifnot(
  abs(unname(check$statistic) - t_observed) < 1e-12,
  abs(unname(check$parameter) - df) < 1e-10
)

data.frame(
  men = length(men), women = length(women),
  mean_men_ms = mean(men), mean_women_ms = mean(women),
  difference_ms = estimate, se_ms = se, t = t_observed, df = df,
  p_value = p_value, lower_ms = interval[1], upper_ms = interval[2]
)
```

The estimated man-minus-woman difference is `r sprintf("%.3f", estimate)` ms, with interval [`r sprintf("%.3f", interval[1])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", interval[2])`] ms.

The formula-to-code bridge is visible in four lines: `v_m` and `v_w` are $s_m^2/n_m$ and $s_w^2/n_w$; `se <- sqrt(v_m + v_w)` computes the standard error; the next expression computes $\nu$; and `qt(0.975, df) * se` supplies the interval margin.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-welch
#| fig-cap: "Raw /I/ durations for distinct adult speakers. Red points mark the group means."
group_means <- aggregate(duration_ms ~ speaker_type, data = hid, mean)

ggplot(hid, aes(speaker_type, duration_ms)) +
  geom_jitter(color = "grey45", alpha = 0.7, width = 0.08, height = 0, # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
              seed = 20261018) +
  geom_point(data = group_means, color = "#8B1A1A", size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Speaker group", y = "/I/ duration in hid (ms)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The comparison is descriptive for these screened cohorts. It does not isolate a causal effect of gender, and the recruitment design does not make either group a probability sample of a wider speaker population.

## Recap and forward link

1. Independence removes the covariance term from the variance of a difference.
2. Welch's procedure estimates the two group variances separately.
3. The approximate degrees of freedom reflect uncertainty in both variance estimates.
4. A descriptive group contrast is not a causal effect of group membership.

The [Fisher exact-test page](fishers-exact-test.qmd#the-conditional-probability) moves from continuous speaker measurements to a finite morphological table.

## Check your understanding

1. Why are the variance contributions added?
2. Which assumption makes the between-group covariance zero?
3. What additional assumption would the pooled-variance t procedure make?
4. Why would matching speakers by row number invent pairing?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. For independent groups the covariance is zero, so the variance of the difference is the sum of the two mean variances. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The assumption that the adult-men and adult-women speaker samples are independent makes the between-group covariance zero. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A pooled-variance procedure would additionally assume equal population variances in the two groups. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Row number has no design-based link across the disjoint speaker groups, so matching on it would fabricate within-pair covariance. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
